unit.title: Finance for marketers
unit.description: P&L, revenue, COGS, gross margin, operating expenses, EBITDA, cash versus profit, prices with and without VAT, budget versus actual, business case, payback, ROI

cards.definition: The summary of a period: revenue, minus cost of goods sold gives the gross margin, minus operating expenses (marketing, salaries, rent) gives the operating result. It shows whether the business makes money.
cards.example: Revenue 1,000,000; COGS 400,000; gross margin 600,000; operating expenses 500,000; operating result 100,000.

cards.definition: Cost of goods sold: the direct costs of what was sold (products bought or made, packaging, sometimes shipping). Marketing is not part of COGS; it is an operating expense.
cards.example: A shop selling a 50 euro jacket bought 20 euros has 20 euros of COGS on that sale.

cards.definition: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization: a common view of operating profitability before financing and accounting choices. In French: EBE is close to it.
cards.example: Investors compare the EBITDA margin of two e-commerce companies.

cards.definition: Operating expenses (opex) are recurring costs of the period, such as ads, salaries, software subscriptions. Capital expenditure (capex) buys assets used for years, such as machines or a custom platform, and is spread over time.
cards.example: A yearly SaaS licence is opex; building a warehouse is capex.

cards.definition: A profitable company can run out of cash: customers pay late, stock is paid upfront, growth needs cash before it brings any. Cash flow decides survival.
cards.example: Big orders in November, paid by customers in January, while suppliers want payment in October.

cards.definition: In France, prices are quoted excluding VAT (HT, hors taxes) in B2B and including VAT (TTC) for consumers. The standard VAT rate is 20 percent: 100 euros HT become 120 euros TTC. Revenue is counted HT.
cards.example: A product sold 60 euros TTC brings 50 euros of revenue HT.

cards.definition: Comparing what was planned with what was really spent and earned, line by line, to explain gaps and reallocate. Finance teams expect marketing to explain variances, not only to spend.
cards.example: Ads were 15 percent over budget in March because of a test; results justify keeping it.

cards.definition: A short document to win a budget: the problem, the proposal, costs, expected gains with assumptions, payback period, risks and how success will be measured.
cards.example: Invest 60,000 euros in a CRM, expected to save 40,000 euros a year: payback in 18 months.

exercises.prompt: Revenue 500,000 euros, COGS 200,000 euros. What is the gross margin?
exercises.explain: Gross margin = revenue minus COGS. Divided by revenue: 60 percent.

exercises.prompt: Where does the advertising budget appear in a P&L?
choices: Nowhere, it is off the books
exercises.explain: Marketing spend is an operating expense, below the gross margin line.

exercises.prompt: A product costs 60 euros TTC for a consumer in France, with 20 percent VAT. What revenue does the shop book?
exercises.explain: 60 divided by 1.2 = 50 euros HT. VAT is collected for the State; it is not revenue.

exercises.prompt: A company is profitable but cannot pay its suppliers. How is it possible?
choices: Cash comes in later than costs go out
It has too many customers paying upfront
exercises.explain: Profit is not cash. Payment delays, stock and fast growth can drain cash in a profitable business.

exercises.prompt: Which is capex rather than opex?
choices: Building a custom e-commerce platform used for years
exercises.explain: Capex creates an asset spread over several years; opex is consumed in the period.

exercises.prompt: You invest 60,000 euros and expect a gain of 3,000 euros of margin per month. What is the payback period?
exercises.explain: 60,000 divided by 3,000. Payback is easy to explain to a finance team; add risks and assumptions.

exercises.prompt: A campaign cost 20,000 euros and generated 50,000 euros of gross margin. What is the ROI?
exercises.explain: ROI = (gain minus cost) divided by cost = 30,000 divided by 20,000. Compute it on margin, not on revenue.

exercises.prompt: A business case should state its assumptions and how success will be measured.
exercises.explain: True. Finance trusts numbers it can check. Assumptions, risks and a measurement plan make a case credible.

exercises.prompt: Ads are 15 percent over budget this month. What does finance expect from you?
choices: An explanation of the gap and a decision on the next months
A new budget twice as large
Hiding the gap in another line
exercises.explain: Budget versus actual reviews are routine. Explain, show the results, and adjust.

exercises.title: Defending the marketing budget
exercises.scenario: The CFO wants to cut marketing by 30 percent. Marketing is 18 percent of revenue; the CEO asks you for a recommendation.

steps.prompt: What do you bring to the meeting first?
choices: Results per channel in margin, with incrementality where measured
The number of followers gained this year
The awards won by the last brand campaign
A list of every tool the marketing team uses
steps.feedback: Speak the language of finance: margin, payback, incremental impact.

steps.prompt: Some spend has no measurable effect. What do you propose?
choices: Cut it yourself and move part of it to proven channels
Ask for more budget on those lines
Hide those lines in a single total
steps.feedback: Proposing your own cuts earns credibility and protects what works.

steps.prompt: How do you present the brand spend that is hard to measure?
choices: As a test plan: geo holdouts and MMM over the year
As a matter of faith in creativity
As free advertising from the media
You do not present it at all
steps.feedback: Turn uncertainty into a measurement plan with dates and decisions.

exercises.explain: A marketer who masters the P&L, margin and payback gets budgets; one who talks only about clicks loses them.
